II C: All simulations were carried out on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. || Sec. IV A: On the 36-site cluster, GCNNs achieve energies extremely close to exact-diagonalisation results for both the nearest-neighbour and maximally frustrated models within a few GPU-hours. || Acknowledgments: Computing resources were provided by STFC Scientific Computing Department's SCARF cluster and STFC Cloud service, as well as the Texas Advanced Computing Center (TACC) at the University of Texas at Austin. || Sec. II A: All GCNN ansätze used in this work have a fixed number of feature maps in every layer, connected by real-valued kernels K, W. In most cases, we restrict the embedding kernels K to the local clusters shown in Fig. 1. We also impose locality on the convolutional kernels W: these are only nonzero for g = t p, where p is a point-group symmetry that leaves the origin in place, and t is a translation by a lattice vector indicated in Fig. 1. || FIG. 1. Arrangement of nonzero kernel entries for the square (left) and triangular (centre) lattices. The cross indicates the origin of the lattice and/or pure point-group symmetries. [figure, counted: triangular 3+4+5+4+3 = 19 entries, square 1+3+5+3+1 = 13 entries, cross included] || Sec. II A: The largest symmetry group for which (1b) is applicable in this basis is the direct product of the space group of the lattice and the Z2 spin parity group generated by P = prod_i sigma^x_i [42]. Irreps of this group are specified by the eigenvalue of P = ±1 and an irrep of the space group. || Sec. I: group-convolutional neural networks (GCNNs) [30,32], which allow us to impose the full space-group symmetry of the problem on the wave functions. || Sec. compute.note: Row-level: the 36-site triangular models (J2 = 0 and J2 = J1/8) were each trained for 12 hours (~1500 SR steps) with 4096 MC samples on a single A100; the paper says '36-site models' collectively, so the 12 h applies to both 36-site runs. Architecture: plain GCNN, 4 layers x 6 feature maps, space-group symmetrized; no parameter count given. Energy = -0.560313(3) per site x 144 (Table III, J2 = 0, N = 36, GCNN column, no Lanczos step). || parameters = 49386 evaluated (4-layer plain GCNN, 36-site triangular, point group C6v order 12): NetKet GCNN with spin parity and input/hidden masks = embedding F*n_in + F bias + (L-1) equivariant layers (F^2*n_h + F bias) + (L-1) parity-flip layers (F^2*n_h, no bias, extra_bias=False default) with F = 6 feature maps, L = 4 layers, n_in = 19 kernel sites (Fig. 1, origin included), n_h = 19 x |point group| 12 = 228: 120 + 24642 + 24624 = 49386. Real parameters ("real-valued kernels"), counted the way NetKet's n_parameters counts them (unmasked entries only, NetKet >= 3.7). Independent of N and of |G|: the masked kernels depend only on the cluster size and the point-group order, so the count changes across rows only through the depth L. Assumptions and their size: (i) spin parity doubles the hidden kernels (the paper's symmetry group is space group x Z2 parity and it labels irreps with ±; without the parity-flip layers the count would be 24762); (ii) biases are the NetKet default use_bias=True (24 parameters; not stated in the paper); (iii) "in most cases" the embedding is local; a full-range embedding (n_in = 36) would give 49488; (iv) with NetKet < 3.7 (e.g. at v1, Nov 2022) masked kernels were stored full-size (F x F x |G|) and multiplied by the mask, so n_parameters would print a larger number of which only the above are free. Consistency check: LayerSR (App. C) requires fewer samples than parameters per layer; with parity one triangular layer pair has 2 x 6 x 6 x 228 + 6 = 16422 parameters, just above the 16384 samples used there, without parity 8214 would not be. Existing samples = 4096 / iterations = 1500 checked: v2 Sec. IV states 4096 samples and approx. 1500 steps for the 36-site models, and the row energy is the v2 value (-0.560313(3) x 144). v1 stated 8192 samples per SR iteration for the 36-site runs (v1 energy -0.56031(7), an earlier run, not this row). Kept 4096.

compute.reported_as: Our best performing model had 4 layers and 16 hidden nodes. We used the Adam optimizer [33] with a learning rate of 3 x 10^-3 and the default parameters. We optimized our learning rate and network architecture on the triangular lattice with J2 = 0.125 and used the same hyperparameters for the other systems, except for the square lattice with J2 = 0 where we found that the learning rate was too high, and decreased it by a factor of 3. Our optimization procedure was as follows. First, we optimized the phase structure for 500 steps by setting Re(log(psi)) = 0 before outputting psi. (...) We then trained both amplitudes and phases for 10^4 steps at batch size 100 before increasing the batch size to 1000 and training for an additional 2 x 10^3 steps. || TABLE III: Comparison between the number of parameters of different equivariant architectures [Connectivity | Nparams]: Full 449856 | Translational 38016 | d6 13056 | Diagonal 1616 || TABLE II: Errors relative to exact diagonalization for 6x6 square-lattice finite-size ground state states.
